props.title: Compounding
lines: Buffett's secret is time, not a magic annual rate.
Linear intuition cannot feel an exponential. That is why compounding confounds.

props.title: Warren Buffett's pile arrived late

rows.v: $84.2 billion of that was accumulated after his 50th birthday.
$81.5 billion came after he qualified for Social Security, in his mid-60s.
Serious investing from age 10. By 30: $1 million then, about $9.3 million inflation-adjusted.
Rough lifetime compounding cited: about 22% a year. Skill is investing. Secret is time.
More than 2,000 books try to explain Buffett. Few stress the calendar.

props.note: Book-dated fortune, not a live Forbes quote.

props.title: Same 22%, far less time

facts.v: $25,000 at age 30, still 22% a year, stop at 60.
99.9% less than the actual book net worth.
The exponential does almost nothing for years, then stands up.

props.note: Counterfactual from the book. The on-screen curve is 22% for 30 years from $25,000.

props.title: Jim Simons versus Buffett, in the book

left.name: Buffett
lines: Started as a child; roughly 75 years of compounding.

right.name: Jim Simons
lines: Renaissance Technologies: about 66% a year since 1988 — roughly 3× Buffett's cited rate.
Found his stride near age 50. Book net worth: about $21 billion — roughly 75% less rich.
If 66% ran for Buffett's 70-year span, the book says the pile becomes tens of quintillions — a joke about time, not a target rate.

props.title: Printed lessons, not a rate chase
items: Most of an exponential's visible work happens in the last years. Stopping early throws away the pile.
A good rate for a long time beats a spectacular rate for a short time — Simons versus Buffett in the book.
You cannot feel compounding with linear intuition. That is why people quit in year eight.
The practical move is staying invested and unbroken — not hunting a 66% personal rate.

props.title: Protect the calendar
items: Most of Buffett's pile arrived after fifty because the years stacked, not because year sixty invented a new trick.
The book's twenty-two percent thought experiment at age thirty still ends near twelve million, not eighty-four billion.
Simons's sixty-six percent is real and rare. Do not treat it as a personal template.
The practical compounding skill is staying unbroken long enough for the curve to bend.
